desc:
A V-shaped array first strictly decreases and then strictly increases: there is an index b with 0 < b < n - 1 such that nums[0] > ... > nums[b] and nums[b] < ... < nums[n - 1].

Given a V-shaped array, return its smallest value (the value at the bottom of the V) in O(log n) time.

For example, [9, 4, 1, 3, 8] has bottom value 1.
constraints: nums is guaranteed to be V-shaped
hints: The smallest value sits where the array stops falling and starts rising.
Compare nums[mid] with nums[mid + 1]. If it is smaller than its right neighbour, you are already on the rising side.
If nums[mid] > nums[mid + 1] the bottom is right of mid (lo = mid + 1); otherwise the bottom is at mid or left of it (hi = mid). Return nums[lo] at the end.
editorial: This is the mirror image of finding the top of a mountain. The test nums[i] > nums[i + 1] ('still falling') holds for every index before the bottom and fails from the bottom onwards, so binary search can find the boundary.

With lo = 0 and hi = n - 1, set mid = (lo + hi) // 2. A falling step means the bottom lies strictly to the right, so lo = mid + 1; a rising step means mid may be the bottom, so hi = mid. When the range shrinks to one index, that index is the bottom.
The running time is O(log n) with O(1) space. The strict slopes matter: a flat stretch would make the 'falling or rising' test ambiguous.
